Foot and ankle injuries are common during athletic activities, not only during contact
and collision sports. Even if these injuries are appropriately managed, many of them may
result in chronic conditions affecting sports participation and daily activities. In addition,
many athlete factors, such as alignment, footwear selection, training regimen, and
metabolic deficiencies, can affect the development and progression of conditions and
injuries of the foot and ankle. Therefore, the treating provider must have an
understanding of the most common injuries, risk factors, and treatment strategies to
managing foot and ankle injuries in athletes. This broad and comprehensive topic is the
focus of entire textbooks. This lesson focuses on the most common foot and ankle
injuries in athletes encountered by orthopaedic surgeons.
Ankle Injuries
Lateral Ankle Sprains and Chronic Instability
Overview and Epidemiology

Overview and Epidemiology
Ankle sprains are among the most common injuries that occur during athletic activities.
The incidence of ankle sprains in the United States is 2.15 per 1,000 person-years.1
Almost one-half of all ankle sprains occur during athletic activity, with basketball,
football, and soccer accounting for the highest incidence of ankle sprains. Lateral ankle
sprains account for 85% of ankle sprains, syndesmotic sprains account for 10% of ankle
sprains, and medial sprains account for 5% of ankle sprains;2 however, this may vary by
sport. Collision sports, such as football and hockey, may be associated with a relatively
higher prevalence of syndesmotic and medial ankle ligament injuries;3 however, lateral
ankle injuries are the most common.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Stability of the ankle joint is a function of extrinsic elements, including ligaments and tendons,
and intrinsic elements, such as the articular geometry of the ankle mortise (Figures 1 and 2;

Resource 1). The contribution of each element varies with load level, the direction in which
force is applied, and the integrity of the ligaments.
The talus is wider anteriorly than posteriorly; therefore, the ankle is most stable in
dorsiflexion and if loaded and is least stable in plantar flexion and if unloaded.
If the ankle is loaded, articular geometry provides 100% of translational stability and 60% of
rotational stability.
The unloaded ankle relies on the ligaments. Between 70% and 80% of anterior stability is
provided by the lateral ligaments, and 50% to 80% of posterior stability is provided by the
deltoid ligaments.
The lateral and deltoid ligaments provide 50% to 80% of rotational stability.4

Risk Factors
Because of the common nature of lateral ligament injuries and the risk of time lost from sports
activities, numerous studies have investigated risk factors associated with ankle sprains.1,5-
8 These risk factors generally can be divided into intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors.
Intrinsic Risk Factors
A recent meta-analysis indicated that the intrinsic factors commonly associated with ankle
sprains include body mass index, slow eccentric inversion strength, fast concentric plantar
flexion strength, passive inversion joint position sense, and reaction time of the peroneus
brevis.5

Cavovarus alignment is a risk factor for ankle sprains (Figure 3).
Age, sex, race, and athletic involvement are risk factors.1
The highest risk of ankle sprains was in females aged 10 to 14 years and males aged 15 to 19
years.
Males aged 15 to 24 years had a higher incidence of lateral ankle injury than females. Athletic
involvement was responsible for 45% to 50% of ankle sprains.
The incidence is substantially higher among Black or White individuals than among Hispanic
individuals.
Additional risk factors commonly assumed to be important include strength, proprioception,
range of motion, and balance.6
A history of an ankle ligament injury is a substantial risk factor for additional ankle sprains in
the ipsilateral and contralateral ankle.7

Extrinsic Risk Factors
Extrinsic risk factors are related to specific sport participation, level of competitiveness, playing
surface, foot alignment, and shoe wear.
Ankle sprains are most common during climbing, indoor volleyball, basketball, and
cheerleading and in field sports, such as rugby, soccer, lacrosse, and American football.
Game competition increases an athlete for an ankle sprain more than practice participation.8

Associated Injuries
Because of the common nature of ankle ligament injuries and chronic ankle instability,
numerous additional injuries are associated with ankle ligament sprains and chronic
instability. Great care should be taken to identify these associated injuries as part of the
diagnosis and management of ankle sprains. Associated injurie include the following:
Peroneal tendon injuries (tears, dislocation, tenosynovitis; Figure 4)
Chondral and osteochondral lesions of the tibial plafond and the talar dome
Intra-articular loose bodies
Anterior/anterolateral ankle soft-tissue impingement
Lateral malleolus ossicles
Syndesmotic injuries
Peroneal nerve injuries
The overall incidence of associated intra-articular lesions is as high as 100% in some studies. In
addition, studies have identified the following associated intra-articular injuries during
arthroscopy.9,10
Synovitis (32% to 100%)
Soft-tissue impingement (14% to 86%)
Chondral injury (22% to 56%)
Osteochondral lesion (7% to 23%)
Lateral malleolus ossicle (25% to 39%)
Anterior osteophyte (11% to 52%)
Intra-articular loose body (1% to 24%)

Associated Injuries
These studies highlight that chronic ankle instability is associated with an extremely high
prevalence of associated intra-articular pathology and shows that arthroscopic
evaluation of the ankle joint during lateral ligament reconstruction is indicated in all
patients to identify intra-articular pathology. Preoperative imaging studies and physical
examination may identify some associated pathology; however, a considerable number
of intra-articular lesions will be missed without arthroscopic evaluation of the joint.

Acute lateral ankle sprains are graded based on the involved ligaments and the severity of the
structural injury to the lateral ligament complex.
A grade I acute sprain is a minor injury to the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL)
characterized by microscopic tears in the ligament fibers without gross structural damage.
A grade II sprain includes partial macroscopic structural damage without complete loss of
integrity.
A grade II sprain primarily affects the ATFL; however, the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL)
may be involved to a lesser extent.
Grade III sprains involve complete rupture of the lateral ligament complex, with loss of
integrity of the ATFL and CFL.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Similar to most musculoskeletal injuries in athletes, successful management of an acute ankle
sprain begins with a careful patient history and physical examination. Important components
of the patient history include the time since injury, mechanism of injury, ability to tolerate
weight bearing, whether the injury is improving, and history of sprains of the same ankle. The
physical examination should document the location and severity of swelling and ecchymosis.
The most important component of the physical examination involves assessing the location
of tenderness to palpation.
After an acute lateral ankle ligament injury, swelling, ecchymosis, and tenderness usually are
noted over the ATFL and CFL in the region just anterior and distal to the tip of the fibula.
Tenderness should be evaluated over several different structures to assess for signs that
may indicate an alternative or concomitant injury.
Surgeon should palpate the distal syndesmosis, lateral malleolus, peroneal tendons, fifth
metatarsal, anterior process of the calcaneus, lateral process of the talus, and the lateral
ligament complex.
Medially, the medial malleolus, deltoid ligament, sustentaculum tali, and navicular should be
examined and assessed for tenderness.
The Achilles tendon, tibialis anterior tendon, and midfoot articulations also should be
routinely palpated; injury to these structures occasionally is neglected if a diagnosis of an
ankle sprain is presumed.

Resistance strength should be assessed via manual muscle testing, particularly the peroneal
tendons.
Palpation during resisted eversion may help to confirm continuity of these structures and aid
in the detection of acute peroneal subluxation or dislocation. Resistance to inversion with the
ankle in a dorsiflexed everted position and circumduction of the ankle are used to improve
the sensitivity of detecting peroneal dislocation.
Many physical examination findings may be obscured by diffuse swelling and poorly localized
tenderness during the first 10 to 14 days after an acute ankle inversion injury.
Repeat the physical examination 10 to 14 days postinjury.
Instability tests, such as the anterior drawer and talar tilt tests, generally do not have an
important role in the evaluation of acute ankle sprains. With an acute injury, the ankle often
is too swollen and uncomfortable to allow for unguarded and accurate assessment of
stability. These tests are most useful to evaluate chronic instability.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Obtaining appropriate radiographs may aid in assessment for associated injuries. In the urgent
care environment, the Ottawa ankle rules provide guidance with regard to whether
radiographs are necessary or can be deferred. Ankle radiographs are indicated if the presence
of a fracture is suggested by tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior edge of the
fibula or the tip of the lateral malleolus, by tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior
edge of the tibia or the tip of the medial malleolus, or by inability to tolerate weight bearing for
at least four steps. In the absence of these findings, the diagnosis usually is an acute sprain,
and radiographs are unnecessary in the general population to reduce costs and irradiation
exposure; however, in radiographs may be an important diagnostic tool in the treatment of
athletes. In addition to identifying associated injuries, radiographs can demonstrate alignment,
avulsion fractures, and some osteochondral injuries. Radiographic and physical examination
findings can be correlated to provide an accurate and complete diagnosis.
Because the treatment plan and return to sport timeline are based on a complete and
accurate diagnosis, the threshold to obtain weight-bearing ankle radiographs (AP, oblique,
lateral views) is lower in athletes.
Additional weight-bearing radiographs of the foot can be obtained if suspicion for a
concomitant foot injury exists based on the patient history or physical examination.

Weight-bearing views provide substantially better images of relevant osseous structures than
non–weight-bearing views and thereby minimize the likelihood of a missed injury.
Simulated weight-bearing views can be obtained on initial evaluation if full–weight bearing is
too painful.
AP and mortise ankle radiographs of the ankle should be evaluated for medial clear space
and syndesmotic widening, malleolar fracture, lateral process of the talus fracture, avulsion
fracture, and talar osteochondral fracture (Figure 5; Resource 2).
Lateral views of the ankle and foot may reveal dorsal talar avulsion fractures, anterior
process of the calcaneus fractures, base of the fifth metatarsal fractures, and os trigonum.

CT has limited indications in the evaluation of acute ankle sprains.
CT is used to detect a suspected associated fracture based on plain radiographic findings;
these include fractures of the lateral process of the talus and the anterior process of
calcaneus, posterior talar fracture, and osteochondral fracture.
CT provides an accurate assessment of fracture size, displacement, and comminution, which
ultimately may guide management.
CT, preferably weight-bearing, also can detect malalignment or displacement of the
syndesmosis via visualization of the clear space in the axial plane.11
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI often is indicated, if available, to evaluate higher-grade ankle sprains in athletes. MRI may
help rule out associated injuries that are difficult to detect on acute examination and
radiographs.
Chondral or osteochondral injury, peroneal tendon injury, nondisplaced fractures, and the
extent of ligamentous injuries
Although identifying the extent of injury and other associated injuries may not always change
the treatment plan, it may be critical for rehabilitation timing and safe return to play. These are
important considerations in athletes. MRI is a reliable and valid diagnostic imaging modality for
surgical planning in patients with ankle instability.12
Management
Nonsurgical Management of Ankle Sprains
The severity of a lateral ankle sprain affects management and prognosis.
Patients with a grade I or grade II sprain typically do not require crutches and are able to
perform activities of daily living with minimal discomfort.
Patients with a grade I or grade II sprain appear to recover best if an early rehabilitation
regimen is implemented.
A recent randomized controlled study demonstrated that patients with a grade I or grade II
sprain achieve earlier recovery if an immediate functional range of motion protocol is
initiated compared with early immobilization.13
The timing of return to sports activity primarily is based on the patient’s level of discomfort
and ability to perform necessary sport-specific activities.

In general, patients can return to sports activity 2 to 6 weeks after a grade I or grade II ankle
sprain with the use of a protective brace and initiation of peroneal strengthening and
proprioceptive exercises aimed at preventing reinjury.
Athletes with a grade III injury may follow a varying course based on anatomy, tissue laxity,
and chronicity of injury.
Grade II injuries are more commonly associated with concomitant injuries. These injuries may
be more painful, limit function, and take longer to recover.
A period of immobilization and protected–weight bearing often is beneficial; however, the
optimal time of immobilization and the exact method of immobilization are not well
established because conflicting results have been reported in various studies.10,14-16
A prospective randomized study compared the efficacy of four different modes of
immobilization (tubular compression sleeve, walking boot, stirrup brace, cast) for the initial
management of acute grade III ankle sprains.14 The results favored initial cast immobilization
for a severe ankle sprain. Patients who underwent initial cast immobilization experienced the
most rapid overall recovery, with less pain and an earlier return to activity.
In athletes, cast immobilization may be suboptimal because it may lead to disuse atrophy,
affecting rapid rehabilitation and return to sports activity. The use of a walking boot was found
to confer no considerable benefit over that of a tubular compression sleeve.
In another randomized trial on the acute management of lateral ankle sprains, the use of a
walking boot for 3 weeks followed by progression to a functional brace was compared with
immediate initiation of functional brace management without any period of immobilization.15
No observed difference was reported between groups in pain or instability.
The immediate functional brace management group had better functional scores and a more
rapid recovery.

Nonsurgical Management of Ankle Sprains
Other evidence-based treatment options for ankle sprains include supervised early
exercise, unsupervised balance-board training, NSAIDs, and a traditional rest-ice-
compression-elevation protocol.8 No scientific evidence supports the use of
ultrasonography, laser therapy, electrotherapy, manual mobilization, extracorporeal
shock wave therapy (ESWT), hyperbaric oxygenation, or platelet-rich plasma (PRP).10

Evidence exists to support bracing or taping during the postinjury period until
rehabilitation is complete.16
Acute Ligament Repair for Severe Ankle Sprains
Extensive data are available on the outcomes of the management of lateral ligament
injuries.8,16 Current opinion, practice patterns, and research studies support functional
nonsurgical management as the preferred method for the management of most lateral ankle
sprains. This recommendation is well supported for grade I and grade II sprains; however,
many variables can affect the outcome and cost-benefit ratio for a patient with a severe grade
III sprain.
Surgical management of a severe sprain leads to a slightly better and more predictable
functional outcomes than nonsurgical management.
Surgical management is more costly and is associated with a higher complication rate than
nonsurgical management.
Functional nonsurgical management leads to a higher incidence of reinjury; however, rates of
return to preinjury status are similar between surgical and nonsurgical management.17
Evidence shows improved excellent outcomes and high rates of return to sports activity after
repair of acute ankle ligament sprains.18,19
Acute ligament repair is preferable for high-grade injuries in professional or elite athletes.20
Surgical Management
The standard surgical management of chronic lateral ankle instability involves the Gould
modification of the Broström procedure.
Anatomic reconstruction of the ATFL and CFL (Figure 6) is associated with good long-term
results
The Broström procedure is associated with limitations related to poor tissue quality, tissue
hypermobility, stresses imposed by large or high-impact athletes, and aggressive early
rehabilitation programs leading to more rapid return to sports activity.21
Several modifications or recommendations should be considered if the Broström-Gould
procedure is used:
Use of an augmentation method for reinforcement and protection
Anatomic allograft reconstruction if local tissue is inadequate

Techniques/Procedures
Augmented Broström procedure
Because of the reliance on healing of native tissues and the risk of stretching these tissues
via aggressive rehabilitation after the Broström procedure, variations of the technique have
been developed to facilitate early range of motion and more aggressive rehabilitation

Anchor-to-anchor suture tape augmentation was developed to facilitate more aggressive
rehabilitation.23
A level III study of patients who underwent repair via this technique showed more rapid
return to activities and improved functional outcome scores.24
Mean time to return to sports activity was 84.1 days, potentially representing an advantage
over nonreinforced anatomic repair.
Functional outcomes were excellent and similar to those reported with other anatomic
repair techniques.
Athletes who are motivated and incentivized to rapidly return to play may benefit from
Broström augmentation with the use of anchor-to-anchor suture tape.23
Although complication rates do not appear to be higher with the augmented technique, the
additional costs should be considered if relevant.
Arthroscopic techniques
All-inside arthroscopic techniques for lateral ligament repair have been developed and
studied as an alternative to the open technique.25,26
In a randomized study comparing all-inside procedures and open procedures, Yeo et al27
found no difference in clinical or radiographic outcomes at a minimum follow-up of 12
months.
Another level III study of 52 ankles in which open or arthroscopic lateral ligament repair was
performed reported less pain and higher functional scores in the arthroscopic group at 6 and
12 months postoperatively, with no complications reported in either group.28
Given the similar outcomes and the advantages of the arthroscopic technique compared
with the open technique, arthroscopic techniques may become more common.
Added costs and inability to access the CFL and peroneal tendons are important
considerations in determining which technique best fits in the treatment armamentarium.
Tendon autograft techniques
The use of tendon autograft techniques is declining as a result of the development of newer
augmented techniques and rehabilitation protocols.
The modified Broström-Evans anatomic-augmented procedure is a proven treatment option
and is associated with excellent clinical results in high-level athletes.29
Stability is added to a standard modified Broström procedure by transferring one-half of
the peroneus brevis tendon to the fibula.
The orientation of this tendon transfer is approximately midway between the ATFL and the
CFL.

The tendon is placed through a bone tunnel in the fibula and is stabilized with the use of an
interference screw to serve as a checkrein against excessive ankle and hindfoot inversion
(Figure 7).
This procedure is particularly useful in high-demand athletes, patients undergoing revision
surgery, and patients with tenuous ligamentous tissue.
The modified Broström-Evans technique has been much more successful than traditional
Evans tenodesis, in which the entire peroneus brevis tendon is transferred to the fibula at a
right angle to the axis of the subtalar joint.
The nonanatomic tenodesis procedure has largely been abandoned because it results in
excessive peroneal weakness and stiffness of the subtalar joint.
Current use of a nonanatomic tenodesis procedure generally is limited to patients with a
neurologic condition and low functional demands.

Medial Ankle Sprains
The medial side of the ankle joint is stabilized by the robust and multi-limb deltoid
ligament. The deltoid is composed of superficial and deep layers with six distinct bands,
of which only the tibionavicular ligament, tibiospring ligament, and deep posterior
tibiotalar ligament are constant. The superficial deltoid is a broad, band-like structure
that originates from the anterior colliculus of the medial malleolus and fans out inferiorly
to insert into the navicular tuberosity, sustentaculum tali, and talar neck (Figure 8). The
deep portion of the deltoid is the primary medial stabilizer of the tibiotalar joint and is
organized into two short, thick, discrete intra-articular bands: the deep anterior tibiotalar
ligament and the deep posterior tibiotalar ligament. The deep posterior tibiotalar
ligament is the largest band of the deltoid complex.30

Biomechanics
The primary function of the deltoid ligament as a whole is to prohibit eversion and abduction.
The deep deltoid also resists external rotation if the foot is dorsiflexed, and it is responsible for
the strongest restraint against lateral translation.

As a robust and multi-limb ligament, the deltoid requires considerable force for disruption
and, therefore, is less commonly injured than the lateral ankle ligaments.
The deep deltoid ligament has a greater load to failure (713.8 N ± 69.3 N) than the lateral
collateral ligaments.31
The superficial deltoid typically fails at the insertion on the medial malleolus, whereas the deep
deltoid ligament typically fails as an intrasubstance rupture near the talar insertion.
Complete rupture of the deltoid ligament is rare in the absence of a syndesmotic or fibular
injury.32
Physical Examination
Because deltoid ligament injuries typically occur via the same mechanism of injury as and
often accompany syndesmotic injuries, the physical examination must always evaluate for
associated syndesmotic injury, lateral ligament injury, and fibular fracture.
During the physical examination, surgeons must pay attention to the proximal fibula because
Maisonneuve injuries can occur.
The flexor tendons—posterior tibial, flexor digitorum longus, and flexor hallucis longus (FHL)—
must be evaluated. Occasionally, associated neurologic injuries to the tibial or saphenous
nerve may occur.
Anterior and posterior translation, medial and lateral translation, internal and external
rotational instability, and varus-valgus instability should be carefully evaluated.
The physical examination is easiest with the patient seated and the knee flexed to 90° and
relaxed.
Comparison with the normal contralateral extremity is important to recognize differences.
Pes planus alignment is a risk factor for deltoid ligament insufficiency.
Medial instability is diagnosed based on medial ankle joint pain; a subjective feeling of giving
way; and instability with anterior translation, external rotation, valgus stress, and in severe
cases posterior translation.
Radiographic Evaluation
Plain radiographs may be suggestive of deltoid ligament injury, especially in patients with an
associated syndesmotic injury or fibular fracture.
A small avulsion fragment maybe present at the tip of the medial malleolus.
A gravity stress radiograph may be useful to detect an acute deltoid injury.

MRI is the preferred imaging modality for defining injury to the deltoid ligaments and
associated structures, with a higher sensitivity and specificity than plain radiographs.33
Management
Most deltoid ligament injuries can be managed nonsurgically in a manner similar to that for
lateral ankle sprains.32
Surgical management typically is dictated by the presence of associated injuries, including
syndesmotic injury, and fractures.
Traditionally, no need exists to repair the injured deltoid ligament because restoration of the
ankle mortise and stabilization of concomitant injuries stabilizes the ankle and allows the
deltoid ligament to heal.
Functional management of grade I and most grade II isolated deltoid sprains via an ankle
brace; a controlled ankle motion walking boot can support the ankle during healing.
The timing of return to sports activity typically is longer than that after a lateral ankle sprain.
An acute grade II or grade III medial sprain does not require surgical management if anatomic
reduction can be maintained via immobilization.

Management
If surgical management is indicated because of an unstable syndesmosis or fibular
fracture, stress fluoroscopy may reveal medial instability. Primary repair of the deltoid
ligament is warranted in this circumstance.34 The use of suture anchors or a suture-only
construct often is adequate to stabilize the medial side of the ankle. Arthroscopic repair
of the deltoid ligament has been described.35
High Ankle Sprains and Syndesmotic Injuries
Overview

located at the level of the tibial plafond. In most patients, the ankle syndesmosis forms a

The wide spectrum of injuries to the syndesmotic complex ranges from subtle sprains to

Local swelling and tenderness after acute injury quickly give way to diffuse signs and

The Cotton, proximal fibular squeeze, external rotation stress, hop, weighted-rotation, and

More than 6 mm of widening of the tibiofibular clear space on an AP radiograph indicates a

MRI is useful for correlating physical examination findings with syndesmotic injury and
predicting time missed from sports activity based on the severity of findings.38

Ankle Impingement Syndromes
Ankle impingement syndromes are common in running and jumping athletes. They may lead
to pain, limited joint motion, and functional limitations. In addition, impinging lesions may
irritate adjacent structures.
Anterior Bony Impingement
Anterior ankle impingement is a common source of pain and limited motion in athletes and is
related to osteophytes on the dorsomedial aspect of the talar neck and the anterolateral
aspect of the distal tibia.
Athletes often have a palpable spur of bone that is painful to palpation and interferes with
performance, particularly during cutting, push-off, and maximum dorsiflexion, which may be
critical in sports such as alpine skiing.
Anterior bony impingement is a consequence of athletic activity that consistently places the
ankle in extreme positions over a long period of time.
A laboratory study of 150 kicking actions by 15 elite football players found that maximal
plantar flexion and stretching of the capsule occurred in only 39% of the kicks; however, direct
trauma to the anteromedial tibia occurred in 76% of the kicks.65
The anterior capsule attaches to the distal tibia a mean of 6 mm proximal to the anterior
cartilage rim rather than near the spurring at the distalmost tibia.66

Anatomy
The Lisfranc, or tarsometatarsal (TMT), joint is the articulation between the base of the five
metatarsals and the three cuneiforms and the cuboid.
Stability primarily is provided by the bone and ligament anatomy.
No ligament exists between the bases of the first and second metatarsals, and stability in this
area mostly depends on the recessed base of the second metatarsal, the Roman arch–wedged
shape of the midfoot arch, and the strong Lisfranc ligament, which connects the medial
cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal.
Pathomechanics
Injuries to the TMT joint are caused by indirect or direct forces.
Indirect forces involve axial loading or twisting on a plantarflexed foot.
Direct injury occurs if a load is applied to the midfoot.
Ligamentous Lisfranc injury commonly occurs in athletes as an injury to the ligaments of the
TMT joints that may extend to the intertarsal joints.
Injuries range from a sprain to an avulsion fracture but usually are not the types of fractures
or dislocations that occur during high-energy injury from a motor vehicle collision or a fall from
a height.
The spectrum of sprains in athletes ranges from a stable sprain without radiographic
displacement to a severe sprain with obvious widening between the base of the first and
second metatarsals or further into the midfoot.
Classification
The classification system described by Nunley and Vertullo86 in a 2002 study is useful in
treating athletes with a relatively mild injury.
In a stage I injury, the patient is unable to participate in sports because of pain in the Lisfranc
joint; weight-bearing radiographs show no displacement, and bone scans or MRIs may be
negative.
A stage II injury involves first-to-second metatarsal diastases of 1 to 5 mm but no evidence of
loss of arch on weight-bearing radiographs.
Stage III injury involves first-to-second metatarsal diastases of more than 5 mm and evidence
of loss of arch on weight-bearing radiographs.

Diagnosis and Workup
Injuries to the TMT joint often are misdiagnosed; therefore, a high index of suspicion is
required.
The diagnosis of a severe injury with displacement usually is obvious; however, a ligamentous
injury with minimal displacement likely will be missed.
Pain with weight bearing should be the first sign if it is accompanied by local swelling and
tenderness at the midfoot.
Even with a mild injury, the athlete has difficulty pushing off. Pronation-abduction or
supination-adduction stress usually is painful.
The physical examination should include evaluation of the dorsalis pedis pulse and deep
peroneal nerve function and assessment for foot compartment syndrome in patients with a
severe Lisfranc fracture-dislocation.
Predisposing factors for Lisfranc injury include a ratio of second metatarsal length to foot
length of less than 29% and a greater second metatarsal length relative to the depth of the
mortise formed by the cuneiforms.88
Diagnostic imaging studies of a foot in which a Lisfranc fracture-dislocation is suspected begins
with AP weight-bearing radiographs and oblique and lateral radiographs (Figure 16).
Comparison with a weight-bearing AP radiograph of the uninjured foot often is helpful. Ten
common radiographic findings are indicative of midfoot injury.89
If a Lisfranc injury is suspected and plain radiographs are not diagnostic, CT or MRI is useful. If
routine radiographs are not diagnostic in patients with a mild injury, stress radiographs or
fluoroscopic images obtained with the patient under anesthesia may be helpful.

Surgical Management
Anatomic reduction is the key to a good outcome in a patient with a Lisfranc injury.
A short leg non–weight-bearing cast is effective in patients with a truly nondisplaced, stable
Lisfranc sprain until tenderness resolves at approximately 6 weeks, with subsequent functional
rehabilitation.
If displacement is present, rigid internal fixation is recommended for the injured TMT joints as
necessary for stability. Screws (Figure 17) or plates can be used for fixation.
Temporary stabilization in anatomic alignment is preferable for the fourth and fifth TMT joints
to preserve their mobility.

The most important negative prognostic factors in patients with a Lisfranc injury are severe
soft-tissue injury and nonanatomic reduction.
Jones Fractures
Fractures of the base of the fifth metatarsal are classified by zone (Figure 18).
Zone 1 represents an avulsion fracture of the lateral tuberosity.
Zone 2 is a Jones-type fracture of the metaphysis or the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction.
Zone 3 is a proximal diaphyseal fracture.
A stress fracture can occur in zone 2 or zone 3, and some experts recommend combining
these two zones because they are associated with a similar risk of delayed union or nonunion
and refracture and surgical management and outcomes are similar.
Blood supply to zone 2 limits healing potential of acute fractures and repetitive stress injuries
to this region, increasing the risk of nonunion in athletes.
Proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures are most common in athletes who participate in
sports such as basketball, football, or soccer.
The patient has worsening activity-related pain along the lateral aspect of the midfoot over a
period of several weeks.

Turf Toe and Hallux Sesamoid Injuries
Turf toe originally was described as a hyperextension injury to the first MTP joint caused by
wearing flexible shoes on hard artificial surfaces; however, the definition has evolved to
encompass almost any injury to the first MTP joint caused by sports participation.
The primary injury involves the plantar plate, or capsuloligamentous complex of the first MTP
joint, which typically is injured in skill-position football players who axially load their heels
with the forefoot fixed on the turf.103
Varus and valgus forces also may contribute to a turf toe injury, further destabilizing the joint
with loss of integrity of the collateral ligaments.
Evaluation
After an acute injury, the athlete has pain, swelling, ecchymosis, and stiffness at the first MTP
joint, which are classified based on severity.104
Initial radiographs are standing weight-bearing AP and lateral views of the foot, which often
appear normal.
The radiographic position of the sesamoids should be compared with that of the contralateral
normal side to detect any retraction.
An avulsion fracture, a sesamoid fracture, or diastasis of bipartite sesamoids also may be
observed. MRI is reliable for assessing the extent of soft-tissue injury (Figure 20).
Biomechanical studies have found that stress fluoroscopy is reliable for diagnosing an
unstable injury.105
Injury to at least three of the four ligaments is indicated by a 3-mm difference in sesamoid
excursion on stress dorsiflexion fluoroscopy compared with that of the uninjured side.106

Management
Nonsurgical management of a turf toe injury begins with a rest-ice-compression-elevation
protocol.
Immobilization is used to control acute swelling and rest the toe.
Early joint mobilization is essential because stiffness is a common sequela of this injury.
Management includes restricting dorsiflexion of the first MTP joint by stiffening the shoe or
using carbon fiber or graphite inserts to reduce the amount of energy transfer from the foot
during push-off.
Taping of the hallux also is useful.
As symptoms allow, the rehabilitation program begins with active and passive non–weight-
bearing and weight-bearing range-of-motion exercises for the foot and ankle.
The ability to return to play is dictated by symptoms and function.
The use of anesthetic agents or steroid injections to allow the athlete to return to play is not
recommended because of the potential for additional joint deterioration or injury.
In patients with a severe injury, first MTP joint stability is compromised. A complete plantar
plate tear, sesamoid retraction, sesamoid fracture or diastasis, traumatic bunion, progressive
hallux valgus or varus, or dislocation of the MTP joint may indicate instability that requires
surgical management.
The joint is stabilized by repairing the pathology, including associated chondral lesions,
fractures, and torn ligaments, and removing loose bodies.

Sesamoid Disorders
The sesamoids of the great toe, which are part of the plantar plate complex, often are involved
in acute traumatic and overuse injuries.
These two small bones undergo considerable force with weight bearing and may be a source
of pain from traumatic fracture with displacement, stress reaction or fracture, sesamoiditis,
osteonecrosis, or osteoarthritis.
Radiographs, including weight-bearing AP comparison views, should be obtained and may be
useful in patients with an acute injury.
A dedicated bone scan and MRIs may be obtained to confirm the diagnosis and determine the
site and extent of the injury.
Management
Management may be a challenge.
Activity and shoe wear modifications are used, with an orthosis used if necessary.
Shock-absorbing shoes with dancer pads may be used to offload the stresses on the
sesamoids and may provide the patient with considerable relief.
NSAIDs, physical therapy, and anesthetic and steroid injections provide considerable pain
relief.
If necessary, a controlled ankle motion walking boot or a toe spica cast can be used for
immobilization.
Surgical treatment is the last treatment option for patients with osteonecrosis and/or
arthrosis. The only surgical treatment options are partial or complete excision of the affected
sesamoid.
Satisfactory outcomes have been reported, especially among athletes.108

Acute Achilles Tendon Rupture
Despite considerable published research, little consensus exists on the optimal management
of Achilles tendon ruptures.
The injury is most common in men who are so-called weekend warrior athletes in their
twenties through forties; however, it can affect individuals regardless of age, sex, or level of
athletic participation (including nonparticipation).
The mechanism of injury most commonly involves a sharp dorsiflexion force onto a tensioned
tendon, which typically creates a rupture through an area of preexisting degenerative change
in the watershed area 2 cm to 6 cm from its insertion.
In a study by Raikin et al,109 acute rupture was missed in 24% of patients, many of whom were
elderly or had a high body mass index.
Based on a careful patient history and physical examination findings, including an abnormal
Thompson test, decreased resting tension, and a palpable gap within the tendon, diagnosis
can reliably be made without more sophisticated imaging studies.110
Ultrasonography and MRI may be useful in patients with ambiguous physical examination
findings, patients with a chronic rupture, or patients in whom objective confirmation of injury
is necessary (Figure 21).

Achilles Tendinopathies
Non-insertional Achilles Tendinopathy
Overuse injuries related to the Achilles tendon are common and include tendinosis,
paratenonitis, superficial and retrocalcaneal bursitis, and insertional Achilles tendinopathy.
Achilles tendinosis is a noninflammatory condition that involves anaerobic intratendinous
degeneration and atrophy, initially is asymptomatic, and results from repetitive microtrauma
or aging.
Pain may represent partial tearing in an area of degenerative tendon and warrants evaluation
and nonsurgical management consisting of rest, the use of a small heel lift or an Achilles
tendon heel pad, correction of hindfoot misalignment, physical therapy, and correction of
training errors.
Ultrasonography and MRI can be performed to evaluate the extent of tendon involvement.
Management
Heavy eccentric calf training is the mainstay of nonsurgical management and is associated
with excellent results.118
Surgical management involves débridement of diseased tissue via a medial or lateral
approach; however, the central tendon-splitting approach has gained favor because it affords
more direct access to the pathology.
Involvement of more than 50% of the tendon or advanced patient age necessitates
augmentation via FHL tendon transfer.

Key Study Points
Ankle sprains are one of the most common athletic injuries. Good evidence from high-level
studies is available to guide treatment decision making.
Suture button devices are associated with superior reduction and better clinical outcomes
compared with screws in the management of unstable syndesmotic injuries.
Osteochondral lesions of the ankle respond poorly to nonsurgical management, and surgical
management continues to evolve.
The causes and locations of ankle impingement are numerous, and open and arthroscopic
procedures are effective.
Plantar fasciitis may be mimicked by a calcaneal stress fracture or tarsal tunnel syndrome.
Anatomic reduction is the most important factor in achieving a good outcome after a Lisfranc
injury.
Surgical fixation is the preferred treatment option for Jones fractures in athletes. Percutaneous
procedures are associated with low risk, and excellent outcomes are achieved in most
patients.
Minimally invasive Achilles tendon repair is associated with more rapid return to sports activity
and lower complication and re-rupture rates.
